header:
Money Myth:
Big Money to Invest?

lines.text: Myth: you need thousands to start investing. Try $1.
lines.say: Myth: you need thousands to start investing. Try one dollar.

lines.text: Yet in 2025, 38% of Americans owned no stock at all.
lines.say: Yet in twenty twenty-five, thirty-eight percent of Americans owned no stock at all.

lines.text: Ownership rose from 52% in 2016 to 62% in 2025. Still, the myth sticks.
lines.say: Ownership has climbed, from fifty-two percent in twenty sixteen to sixty-two percent in twenty twenty-five, but the myth sticks.

scene.title: % of US adults who own stock

lines.text: The workaround: fractional shares. You buy a slice of a share with dollars.
lines.say: The workaround is fractional shares, where you buy a slice of one share with dollars.

lines.text: Fidelity's minimum is $1. Schwab's is $5 per S&P 500 stock.
lines.say: At Fidelity, a slice starts at one dollar, and at Schwab it's five dollars per S and P five hundred stock.

lines.text: $10 into a $250 share = 0.04 of a share, plus 4% of any dividend.
lines.say: So ten dollars into a two-hundred-fifty-dollar share buys four hundredths of it, plus four percent of any dividend it pays.

lines.text: Even the US Treasury sells I bonds from $25 and T-bills from $100.
lines.say: Even the US Treasury sells I bonds from twenty-five dollars and Treasury bills from one hundred.

lines.text: $5 a week is $260 a year. The habit matters more than the amount.
lines.say: Five dollars a week adds up to two hundred sixty dollars a year, so the habit matters more than the starting amount.

lines.text: That's the money. Follow for more.
lines.say: That's the money. Follow for more.

post.title: You don't need thousands to invest. Try $1.
post.ig:
Myth: you need thousands to start investing.
Fidelity's fractional shares start at $1; Schwab Stock Slices start at $5 per S&P 500 stock.
TreasuryDirect sells I bonds from $25 and T-bills from $100.
Yet 38% of Americans owned no stock in 2025 (Gallup).
Sources: Fidelity, Schwab, TreasuryDirect, Gallup.
